title: The Endurance of François K
summary: A conversation about late-1970s New York, the dancefloor as a space for community and François Kevorkian’s contemporary work reconstructing classic recordings live.
transcript:
Listening just there to the definitive dancefloor anthem Go Bang, the François K mix. Legend has it that François K was brought in by Arthur Russell in 1982 to fix the original album version, which DJs apparently found too complex. And François Kevorkian, aka François K, famously mixed it on borrowed time at Right Track Studios to create the version we were just listening to.

There was an opportunity to chat yesterday over Zoom, which we were extremely thrilled and honoured to have. François K is currently touring the country, with a highly anticipated set scheduled for the Golden Plains 18 festival next week, March 7. There's going to be a club show at Melbourne's The Quadraphonic Club as well on March 6, and this Saturday an extraordinary opportunity to see the pioneer play at Federation Square. It's going to be a free gig that takes place in the evening time.

Let's check the details. Yeah, I think it all kicks off 6 p.m., goes till 9:30. There's going to be François K as well as Σtella, who's signed to the Seattle indie label Sub Pop, channelling Greek pop, vintage synths and cinematic storytelling, and Ganavya, the New York-born, California-raised vocalist and composer, also performing.

I suppose to give a little bit of context to anyone arriving more recently to François K's music: he arrived in New York City in September 1975 with no money, apparently, and nowhere to stay. He trained as a jazz drummer in France under Tony Williams, who was Miles Davis's drummer, and decided at the age of 21 that New York was where he needed to be.

So within two years he was holding the Saturday-night residency at New York New York, one of the city's premier clubs, and within three years he was at Prelude Records, where his remix of Musique's In the Bush became a huge hit. Through the early 80s he held the record for the most number of number-one 12-inch singles on Billboard's dance music chart: records by Yazoo, D-Train, Sharon Redd and Dinosaur L, which we were listening to.

One of the only DJs ever invited to play at Paradise Garage, The Loft and Better Days, which were the three spaces that really defined New York's underground in that era. He was a very close friend and collaborator of Larry Levan, another pioneering figure. Others might know François K because he mixed Depeche Mode's Violator in 1990, a record which sold somewhere between seven and 25 million copies, depending on which charts you look at.

He had a studio in the same building as [venue name uncertain: Studio 51], has founded parties that continue to this day with his friends Danny Krivit and Joe Claussell, worked with Haruomi Hosono of Yellow Magic Orchestra, played the closing set at Space Lab Yellow in Tokyo — a set that ran for more than 30 hours — and he turned 71 in January.

He's still playing those sort of marathon sets, seven and eight hours. He streams often on Twitch, four-hour sessions at a time. He's got a monthly radio show on Worldwide FM. He's writing an autobiography, got a documentary in the works about that New York underground scene. And I guess something that comes up in this interview is also his pioneering of a technique that he calls Live Stems, where he uses machine learning to separate the individual elements of classic recordings and to reconstruct them on stage, improvised.

[Unclear audio at 00:03:51–00:03:54]

One thing I've observed throughout the arc of a pretty long career is that I tend to pick different things at different times and not stay focused on the same thing over and over. And that probably accounts for why I always find something that's really exciting, because it always feels kind of fresh.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:37–00:04:42]

One of the ways that curiosity is expressing itself right now is through a technique that he calls Live Stems, where he uses machine learning to pull apart classic recordings. He loads them into separate players and he rebuilds the whole thing live, so it's improvising. This is the technique and the philosophy in his words.

[Unclear audio at 00:05:01–00:05:11]

And it's very gratifying because I'm able to use this to bring music that people know, are familiar with, and perform it in a unique and never-again-will-be-heard-in-the-same-way kind of fashion, totally improvised in front of them.

So what it means is that I'm able to create endless variations and new versions of things they've heard forever, in ways that are very endearing and, you know, that kind of bring me back to the beginning of what we were doing manually in the studio 45 years ago, when computers were not part of the equation.

And again, what I'm doing right now, it's all live. It's all done on the fly in front of people, in the moment. And I think there's an incredible value to this.

[Unclear audio at 00:05:59–00:06:25]

[Unclear audio at 00:06:41–00:06:44]

Talking about what keeps him curious and motivated 50 years into his career, I suppose looking back, we asked him next about where that education really began: New York City in the late 1970s and three clubs that shaped, in many ways, everything that came afterwards — Paradise Garage, The Loft and Better Days. We talked a little bit about what it meant to move through those spaces and what he's carried from them into his work today.

[Unclear audio at 00:07:08–00:07:11]

Back in that time, not just in New York City, but the whole entire world was very different. And while I think there's today a large number of people who equate disco with Boney and ABBA and Village People — over-the-top commercial groups that, you know, arguably had very, very successful runs of hot disco kind of things — to us in New York City back in the early 80s, it really was about a type of music that was much more futuristic to us back then.

It still blended all the traditional and classic influences of soul music, of Motown, of Stax, of all the great R&B, soul and other types of music that reflected the Black experience. And we were able to congregate in places that those mainstream people I spoke about before would have never been interested in, because it was a different kind of community.

And even though now, today, these places have gained great significance, you could argue that even though they were extremely influential, because they influenced major radio stations like WBLS, which was basically one of the top radios in America, and…

[Unclear audio at 00:08:39–00:09:10]

They had an oppressive breath of a culture that basically marginalized them, and this is where all of that is born from. And I think part of the reason why it still remains as vital as it does today is because, beyond being the expression of a specific cultural viewpoint, it represented a lifeline for a lot of those who went to these venues.

[Unclear audio at 00:10:05–00:10:09]

I think that, to some degree, that is still somehow valid today, especially with the LGBTQ communities. You know, you could argue that this is still the case in many places around the world. So I don't find it that different, to be honest, because I tend to gravitate around those kinds of places today.

Like, say for example, just last weekend I was in Toronto, where I did a back-to-back six-hour set with Colleen 'Cosmo' Murphy. The next day was Theo Parrish doing a 10-hour set all afternoon, at a venue called Standard Time in Toronto. And again, it's kind of the same pattern of people who are more on the artistic side of things and, you know…

[Unclear audio at 00:10:57–00:10:59]

More on what we call, loosely, underground, sort of finding places where they feel it's totally great to congregate and be away from the air-quote mainstream, if we could call it. I think that's what it's always been about.

And not to deny that sometimes certain people have had massive hits, like Chic, Good Times, for example, or records like that that completely crossed over. But at the beginning, at the core of it, I think dance music and disco was a social phenomenon. And I think it reflected the idea that inclusiveness, diversity and so much more were part of the core values of what we should try to espouse. And sadly, given what we see around the world with certain political movements, I think it's still as relevant as ever.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:41–00:12:45]

Sometimes I'll play certain things that might shock people: a harsh drum and bass record right in the middle of a disco set, or playing a reggae track or dancehall right in the middle of something that was more like house, you know, just because I feel it's needed or necessary.

But I'd rather you remember those moments, or me playing a Killing Joke record in the middle of something that was more electronic or whatever. I'd rather you remember those moments, even if you didn't really appreciate them for what they were, instead of leaving the gig not remembering anything because it was all perfectly streamlined, insipid, and only designed for the moment and not for anything else but that.

So that's really a choice, and I think I've kind of cast my fate to the wind with that a long time ago, because I'm kind of known for doing things like this. So are certain other DJs. Certainly, I can think of Laurent Garnier as being someone who's kind of known for doing this. But, you know, that's the person I am. If I want to play a Hendrix record in the middle of what I'm doing, I will do it.

And sadly, I think that with the pressures of modern life, social media, mass exposure, a lot of DJs have become very, very risk-averse, whether it's because their manager is telling them not to do it, or because they want to get booked again, or this or that, who knows.

But I think, at the core of it, what strikes me as very important is to never forget that connection with people, and that part of what we should be doing is to express thoughts, ideas and artistic concepts that somehow can inspire others instead of keeping them just sedated.

[Unclear audio at 00:14:29–00:14:32]
